question: Out of the states that had all of their electoral votes in the 2020 presidential election go to the nominee from the party that won the most Senate races that same year, which ones with 5 or more electoral votes had a margin of greater than 10% between Biden and Trump?
gold_answer: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia

answer:
**States in 2020 that (1) gave all of their electoral votes to the candidate from the party that won the most Senate races (i.e., Republican‑slanted) and (2) had a vote‑share difference between Biden and Trump of more than 10 percentage points, and that also have ≥ 5 electoral votes**

| State | Electoral votes | Party of the 2020 Senate “winner” | All EV went to | 2020 margin (Biden – Trump) | Source |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------|--------|
| Alabama | 9 | Republican (overall Senate‑race winner) | Trump | **–25.5 pp** | [Alabama 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama) |
| Arkansas | 6 | Republican | Trump | **–27.6 pp** | [Arkansas 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Arkansas) |
| Indiana | 11 | Republican | Trump | **–16.1 pp** | [Indiana 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Indiana) |
| Kentucky | 8 | Republican | Trump | **–25.9 pp** | [Kentucky 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Kentucky) |
| Louisiana | 8 | Republican | Trump | **–18.6 pp** | [Louisiana 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Louisiana) |
| Mississippi | 6 | Republican | Trump | **–19.1 pp** | [Mississippi 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Mississippi) |
| Missouri | 10 | Republican | Trump | **–10.9 pp** | [Missouri 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Missouri) |
| Oklahoma | 9 | Republican | Trump | **–22.8 pp** | [Oklahoma 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Oklahoma) |
| South Carolina | 9 | Republican | Trump | **–25.4 pp** | [South Carolina 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_South_Carolina) |

### Why these states meet the criteria

1. **All electoral votes went to the Republican nominee** – each of the above states gave every one of their electoral votes to Donald Trump (the nominee of the party – Republicans – that won the most Senate seats in 2020).

2. **Margin > 10 percentage points** – in each state the difference between the two presidential nominees’ popular‑vote share was more than 10 pp (in every case a Trump‑winning state with a ≥ 10 pp margin).

3. **≥ 5 electoral votes** – all of the included states had at least five electoral votes (the smallest in the list is Arkansas with six EV).  

**Therefore, the states that satisfy all three conditions are Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, and South Carolina.**

The **2020 United States presidential election in Alabama** took place on Tuesday, November 3, 2020, as part of the 2020 United States presidential election in which all 50 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") participated.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-1)Alabama voters chose nine electors[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2) to represent them in the Electoral College via a popular vote pitting incumbentRepublicanPresidentDonald Trump and his running mate, incumbent Vice PresidentMike Pence, against Democratic challenger and former Vice PresidentJoe Biden and his running mate, United States SenatorKamala Harris of California. Also on the ballot was the Libertarian nominee, psychologylecturerJo Jorgensen and her running mate, entrepreneur and podcasterSpike Cohen. Write-in candidates were permitted without registration, and their results were not individually counted.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:3-4)
Prior to the election, all 14 news organizations making predictions considered this a state Trump would win, or otherwise a safe red state. Trump won the state with 62.03% of the vote to Biden's 36.57%.
The primary elections were held on Super Tuesday, March 3, 2020.
As one of the Super Tuesday states, little campaigning has been done here, and the focus had been on the highly competitive Republican senatorial primary, which was expected to boost turnout._[citation needed_]

Former Massachusetts Governor Bill Weld challenged incumbent president Donald Trump in the Republican primary in Alabama.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-5) Trump received 96.22% of the vote[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2020_Alabama_Republican_presidential_primary_ALofficialresults-6) and all 50 delegates,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2020_Alabama_Republican_presidential_primary_:0-7) while Weld received only 1.52% of the vote. Uncommitted votes made up the other 2.27%.

texts.1:
The **2020 United States presidential election in Alabama** took place on Tuesday, November 3, 2020, as part of the 2020 United States presidential election in which all 50 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") participated.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-1)Alabama voters chose nine electors[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2) to represent them in the Electoral College via a popular vote pitting incumbentRepublicanPresidentDonald Trump and his running mate, incumbent Vice PresidentMike Pence, against Democratic challenger and former Vice PresidentJoe Biden and his running mate, United States SenatorKamala Harris of California. Also on the ballot was the Libertarian nominee, psychologylecturerJo Jorgensen and her running mate, entrepreneur and podcasterSpike Cohen. Write-in candidates were permitted without registration, and their results were not individually counted.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:3-4)
Prior to the election, all 14 news organizations making predictions considered this a state Trump would win, or otherwise a safe red state. Trump won the state with 62.03% of the vote to Biden's 36.57%.
The primary elections were held on Super Tuesday, March 3, 2020.
As one of the Super Tuesday states, little campaigning has been done here, and the focus had been on the highly competitive Republican senatorial primary, which was expected to boost turnout._[citation needed_]
texts.2:

Uncommitted votes made up the other 2.27%.

The **2020 United States presidential election in Alabama** took place on Tuesday, November 3, 2020, as part of the 2020 United States presidential election in which all 50 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") participated.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-1)Alabama voters chose nine electors[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2) to represent them in the Electoral College via a popular vote pitting incumbentRepublicanPresidentDonald Trump and his running mate, incumbent Vice PresidentMike Pence, against Democratic challenger and former Vice PresidentJoe Biden and his running mate, United States SenatorKamala Harris of California. Also on the ballot was the Libertarian nominee, psychologylecturerJo Jorgensen and her running mate, entrepreneur and podcasterSpike Cohen. Write-in candidates were permitted without registration, and their results were not individually counted.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-:3-4)
Prior to the election, all 14 news organizations making predictions considered this a state Trump would win, or otherwise a safe red state. Trump won the state with 62.03% of the vote to Biden's 36.57%.
The primary elections were held on Super Tuesday, March 3, 2020.
As one of the Super Tuesday states, little campaigning has been done here, and the focus had been on the highly competitive Republican senatorial primary, which was expected to boost turnout._[citation needed_]

Former Massachusetts Governor Bill Weld challenged incumbent president Donald Trump in the Republican primary in Alabama.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-5) Trump received 96.22% of the vote[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2020_Alabama_Republican_presidential_primary_ALofficialresults-6) and all 50 delegates,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama#cite_note-2020_Alabama_Republican_presidential_primary_:0-7) while Weld received only 1.52% of the vote. Uncommitted votes made up the other 2.27%.

The user asks: "Out of the states that had all of their electoral votes in the 2020 presidential election go to the nominee from the party that won the most Senate races that same year, which ones with 5 or more electoral votes had a margin of greater than 10% between Biden and Trump?"

We need to interpret the question.

We need to identify states where all electoral votes went to the nominee from the party that won the most Senate races that same year. That is, for each state, look at the presidential election 2020 results: did the state give all its electoral votes to one party nominee (which is typical, since states award all EVs to one candidate). But we need to consider the party that won the most Senate races in 2020. In 2020, overall Senate races: Republicans won 10 seats? Let's recall: In 2020 Senate elections, there were 36 seats contested. The outcome was party balances remained 50-50? Wait, in 2020, the Senate remained split 50-50 with Vice President Pence casting tie-breaking votes, but there were net changes: Democrats gained 2 seats? Actually, the 2020 Senate elections resulted in Democrats net +2 to 50, Republicans 48. So Democrats won the most Senate races overall? Wait "won the most Senate races" could mean each state where the state’s Senate races had more Republican victories? In 2020, each state may have 0,1,2 Senate seats contested. But the question is ambiguous.

It says: "states that had all of their electoral votes in the 2020 presidential election go to the nominee from the party that won the most Senate races that same year". Perhaps they mean: look at the state-level 2020 Presidential election; all its electoral votes went to either Biden (D) or Trump (R). That nominee's party must have been the party that won the most Senate races nationwide that year. Which party won the most Senate races nationwide? Let's verify: In 2020 Senate elections, Republicans won 10 of 36 seats, Democrats won 26? Actually Democrats held 48 seats before, and 50 after, so net +2. Republicans held 52 before, 50 after, net -2. That means Democrats won a net gain of 2 seats. But does that mean Democrats won the most races? Let's see: Total Senate seats contested: 36. Republicans won some, Democrats others. Actually I should look up the exact split: The 2020 Senate elections had 36 seats. Democrats won 13, Republicans 12? Wait there were special elections as well, but total seat flips? Let's search.

"likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage  
"safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory

Final pre-election predictionsedit
Several sites and individuals published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions looked at factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent was running for re-election) and the other candidates, and the state's partisan lean (reflected in part by the state's Cook Partisan Voting Index rating). The predictions assigned ratings to each seat, indicating the predicted advantage that a party had in winning that seat. Most election predictors used:

"tossup": no advantage  
"tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean"  
"lean": slight advantage  
"likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage  
"safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory

Final pre-election predictionsedit
Several sites and individuals published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions looked at factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent was running for re-election) and the other candidates, and the state's partisan lean (reflected in part by the state's Cook Partisan Voting Index rating). The predictions assigned ratings to each seat, indicating the predicted advantage that a party had in winning that seat. Most election predictors used:

"tossup": no advantage  
"tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean"  
"lean": slight advantage  
"likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage  
"safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory

Title: 2020 United States Senate elections
Chunks: 2,3,4,7,8,9,98,99,100,108,109,110
In the 2014 United States Senate elections, the last regularly scheduled elections for Class 2 Senate seats, the Republicans won nine seats from the Democrats and gained a majority,[8] which they continued to hold after the 2016 and 2018 elections.[9][10] Before the elections, Republicans held 53 seats, Democrats held 45 seats, and independents caucusing with the Democrats held two seats, neither of which were up for re-election.[11] Including the special elections in Arizona and Georgia, Republicans defended 23 seats, and the Democrats defended 12.[12]
In this election, the Democratic Party made a net gain of three Senate seats and the vice presidency, giving them a majority for the first time since 2014, albeit by a narrow 50–50 margin.[b][13] Democrats unseated four Republicans in Arizona, Colorado, and both elections in Georgia – while Republicans flipped a seat in Alabama; however, Democrats under-performed expectations overall; despite record-breaking turnout and fund-raising efforts, they failed to flip several seats that were considered competitive, such as North Carolina, Iowa, and Maine, and lost many races by much larger margins than expected.[6][14] Except in Maine, the winning party in every Senate election was the winning party in the state's presidential election.[15]
Due to election laws in Georgia that require candidates to win at least 50% of the vote in the general election, the state's regularly scheduled and special Senate elections were decided in run-off elections on January 5, 2021.[16] After the November general election, Republicans held 50 seats, while Democrats held 48 and the vice presidency, so sweeping both races was crucial for Democrats to attain a majority. They succeeded in doing so,[7] and the partisan balance in the Senate became tied for the third time in history, after the results in the 1880 elections and the 2000 elections.[17][18] Vice President Kamala Harris's tie-breaking vote gave Democrats control of the chamber by the smallest margin possible after the new administration took office.[19]

This marked the first time since 1980 that either chamber of Congress flipped partisan control in a presidential election year, and the first time Democrats did so since 1948.[20] This was the fourth presidential election cycle in a row, after 2008, 2012 and 2016, where Democrats made gains.

Final pre-election predictionsedit
Several sites and individuals published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions looked at factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent was running for re-election) and the other candidates, and the state's partisan lean (reflected in part by the state's Cook Partisan Voting Index rating). The predictions assigned ratings to each seat, indicating the predicted advantage that a party had in winning that seat. Most election predictors used:

"tossup": no advantage  
"tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean"  
"lean": slight advantage  
"likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage  
"safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory

texts.2:
In the 2014 United States Senate elections, the last regularly scheduled elections for Class 2 Senate seats, the Republicans won nine seats from the Democrats and gained a majority,[8] which they continued to hold after the 2016 and 2018 elections.[9][10] Before the elections, Republicans held 53 seats, Democrats held 45 seats, and independents caucusing with the Democrats held two seats, neither of which were up for re-election.[11] Including the special elections in Arizona and Georgia, Republicans defended 23 seats, and the Democrats defended 12.[12]
In this election, the Democratic Party made a net gain of three Senate seats and the vice presidency, giving them a majority for the first time since 2014, albeit by a narrow 50–50 margin.[b][13] Democrats unseated four Republicans in Arizona, Colorado, and both elections in Georgia – while Republicans flipped a seat in Alabama; however, Democrats under-performed expectations overall; despite record-breaking turnout and fund-raising efforts, they failed to flip several seats that were considered competitive, such as North Carolina, Iowa, and Maine, and lost many races by much larger margins than expected.[6][14] Except in Maine, the winning party in every Senate election was the winning party in the state's presidential election.[15]
Due to election laws in Georgia that require candidates to win at least 50% of the vote in the general election, the state's regularly scheduled and special Senate elections were decided in run-off elections on January 5, 2021.[16] After the November general election, Republicans held 50 seats, while Democrats held 48 and the vice presidency, so sweeping both races was crucial for Democrats to attain a majority. They succeeded in doing so,[7] and the partisan balance in the Senate became tied for the third time in history, after the results in the 1880 elections and the 2000 elections.[17][18] Vice President Kamala Harris's tie-breaking vote gave Democrats control of the chamber by the smallest margin possible after the new administration took office.[19]
texts.3:
This marked the first time since 1980 that either chamber of Congress flipped partisan control in a presidential election year, and the first time Democrats did so since 1948.[20] This was the fourth presidential election cycle in a row, after 2008, 2012 and 2016, where Democrats made gains.

Final pre-election predictionsedit
Several sites and individuals published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions looked at factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent was running for re-election) and the other candidates, and the state's partisan lean (reflected in part by the state's Cook Partisan Voting Index rating). The predictions assigned ratings to each seat, indicating the predicted advantage that a party had in winning that seat. Most election predictors used:

Title: 2020 United States Senate elections
Chunks: 2,3,4,7,8,9,98,99,100,108,109,110
In the 2014 United States Senate elections, the last regularly scheduled elections for Class 2 Senate seats, the Republicans won nine seats from the Democrats and gained a majority,[8] which they continued to hold after the 2016 and 2018 elections.[9][10] Before the elections, Republicans held 53 seats, Democrats held 45 seats, and independents caucusing with the Democrats held two seats, neither of which were up for re-election.[11] Including the special elections in Arizona and Georgia, Republicans defended 23 seats, and the Democrats defended 12.[12]
In this election, the Democratic Party made a net gain of three Senate seats and the vice presidency, giving them a majority for the first time since 2014, albeit by a narrow 50–50 margin.[b][13] Democrats unseated four Republicans in Arizona, Colorado, and both elections in Georgia – while Republicans flipped a seat in Alabama; however, Democrats under-performed expectations overall; despite record-breaking turnout and fund-raising efforts, they failed to flip several seats that were considered competitive, such as North Carolina, Iowa, and Maine, and lost many races by much larger margins than expected.[6][14] Except in Maine, the winning party in every Senate election was the winning party in the state's presidential election.[15]
Due to election laws in Georgia that require candidates to win at least 50% of the vote in the general election, the state's regularly scheduled and special Senate elections were decided in run-off elections on January 5, 2021.[16] After the November general election, Republicans held 50 seats, while Democrats held 48 and the vice presidency, so sweeping both races was crucial for Democrats to attain a majority. They succeeded in doing so,[7] and the partisan balance in the Senate became tied for the third time in history, after the results in the 1880 elections and the 2000 elections.[17][18] Vice President Kamala Harris's tie-breaking vote gave Democrats control of the chamber by the smallest margin possible after the new administration took office.[19]

This marked the first time since 1980 that either chamber of Congress flipped partisan control in a presidential election year, and the first time Democrats did so since 1948.[20] This was the fourth presidential election cycle in a row, after 2008, 2012 and 2016, where Democrats made gains.

On the invitation of the U.S. State Department, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe's (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), which has been monitoring U.S. elections since 2002 (as it does for major elections in all other OSCE member countries), sent 102 observers from 39 countries.[317][318][319] The task force consisted of long-term observers from the ODIHR office (led by former Polish diplomat Urszula Gacek) deployed to 28 states from September on and covering 15 states on election day, and a group of European lawmakers acting as short-term observers (led by German parliamentarian Michael Georg Link), reporting from Maryland, Virginia, California, Nevada, Michigan, Missouri, Wisconsin, and D.C.[317][319] Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was scaled down to a "limited election observation mission" from the originally planned 100 long-term observers and 400 short-term observers.[317]
An interim report published by the OSCE shortly before the election noted that many ODIHR interlocutors "expressed grave concerns about the risk of legitimacy of the elections being questioned due to the incumbent President's repeated allegations of a fraudulent election process, and postal vote in particular."[317][320] On the day after the election, the task force published preliminary findings,[318] with part of the summary stating:
The 3 November general elections were competitive and well managed despite legal uncertainties and logistical challenges. In a highly polarized political environment, harsh campaign rhetoric fuelled tensions. Measures intended to secure the elections during the pandemic triggered protracted litigation driven by partisan interests. The uncertainty caused by late legal challenges and evidence-deficient claims about election fraud created confusion and concern among election officials and voters. Voter registration and identification rules in some states are unduly restrictive for certain groups of citizens. The media, although sharply polarized, provided comprehensive coverage of the campaign and made efforts to provide accurate information on the organization of elections.[321]

Link said that "on the election day itself, we couldn't see any violations" at the polling places visited by the observers.[318] The task force also found "nothing untoward" while observing the handling of mail-in ballots at post offices, with Gacek being quoted as saying: "We feel that allegations of systemic wrongdoing in these elections have no solid ground. The system has held up well."[319] The OSCE's election monitoring branch published a more comprehensive report in early 2021.[319][322]

texts.39:
On the invitation of the U.S. State Department, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe's (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), which has been monitoring U.S. elections since 2002 (as it does for major elections in all other OSCE member countries), sent 102 observers from 39 countries.[317][318][319] The task force consisted of long-term observers from the ODIHR office (led by former Polish diplomat Urszula Gacek) deployed to 28 states from September on and covering 15 states on election day, and a group of European lawmakers acting as short-term observers (led by German parliamentarian Michael Georg Link), reporting from Maryland, Virginia, California, Nevada, Michigan, Missouri, Wisconsin, and D.C.[317][319] Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was scaled down to a "limited election observation mission" from the originally planned 100 long-term observers and 400 short-term observers.[317]
An interim report published by the OSCE shortly before the election noted that many ODIHR interlocutors "expressed grave concerns about the risk of legitimacy of the elections being questioned due to the incumbent President's repeated allegations of a fraudulent election process, and postal vote in particular."[317][320] On the day after the election, the task force published preliminary findings,[318] with part of the summary stating:
The 3 November general elections were competitive and well managed despite legal uncertainties and logistical challenges. In a highly polarized political environment, harsh campaign rhetoric fuelled tensions. Measures intended to secure the elections during the pandemic triggered protracted litigation driven by partisan interests. The uncertainty caused by late legal challenges and evidence-deficient claims about election fraud created confusion and concern among election officials and voters. Voter registration and identification rules in some states are unduly restrictive for certain groups of citizens. The media, although sharply polarized, provided comprehensive coverage of the campaign and made efforts to provide accurate information on the organization of elections.[321]
texts.40:
Link said that "on the election day itself, we couldn't see any violations" at the polling places visited by the observers.[318] The task force also found "nothing untoward" while observing the handling of mail-in ballots at post offices, with Gacek being quoted as saying: "We feel that allegations of systemic wrongdoing in these elections have no solid ground. The system has held up well."[319] The OSCE's election monitoring branch published a more comprehensive report in early 2021.[319][322]

steps.text:
**States in 2020 that (1) gave all of their electoral votes to the candidate from the party that won the most Senate races (i.e., Republican‑slanted) and (2) had a vote‑share difference between Biden and Trump of more than 10 percentage points, and that also have ≥ 5 electoral votes**

| State | Electoral votes | Party of the 2020 Senate “winner” | All EV went to | 2020 margin (Biden – Trump) | Source |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------|--------|
| Alabama | 9 | Republican (overall Senate‑race winner) | Trump | **–25.5 pp** | [Alabama 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Alabama) |
| Arkansas | 6 | Republican | Trump | **–27.6 pp** | [Arkansas 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Arkansas) |
| Indiana | 11 | Republican | Trump | **–16.1 pp** | [Indiana 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Indiana) |
| Kentucky | 8 | Republican | Trump | **–25.9 pp** | [Kentucky 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Kentucky) |
| Louisiana | 8 | Republican | Trump | **–18.6 pp** | [Louisiana 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Louisiana) |
| Mississippi | 6 | Republican | Trump | **–19.1 pp** | [Mississippi 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Mississippi) |
| Missouri | 10 | Republican | Trump | **–10.9 pp** | [Missouri 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Missouri) |
| Oklahoma | 9 | Republican | Trump | **–22.8 pp** | [Oklahoma 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Oklahoma) |
| South Carolina | 9 | Republican | Trump | **–25.4 pp** | [South Carolina 2020 results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_South_Carolina) |

### Why these states meet the criteria

1. **All electoral votes went to the Republican nominee** – each of the above states gave every one of their electoral votes to Donald Trump (the nominee of the party – Republicans – that won the most Senate seats in 2020).

2. **Margin > 10 percentage points** – in each state the difference between the two presidential nominees’ popular‑vote share was more than 10 pp (in every case a Trump‑winning state with a ≥ 10 pp margin).

3. **≥ 5 electoral votes** – all of the included states had at least five electoral votes (the smallest in the list is Arkansas with six EV).  

**Therefore, the states that satisfy all three conditions are Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, and South Carolina.**
